what: Secret-shaped strings that the history sweep finds, and which are known to be decoys rather than leaks.
why: A security sweep that cries wolf is the one nobody reads. But dropping its findings in silence is worse: a real key sitting in a test file would go out with them. So every finding is either declared here, with a reason, or it fails the check.
howItMatches: A declaration covers one form, in one file, for one value — matched by the SHA-256 prefix of the exact string found. Declaring by form and file alone would excuse any AWS key ever dropped into that file, which would open a false green while closing nothing.
whatItIsNotFor: A real secret is never declared here. A real secret is in the history for good, and the answer is to REVOKE it at the provider, not to record it as acceptable.

entries.pourquoi: The example access key AWS itself publishes in its own documentation — issued to nobody, valid nowhere. It is the positive control for the sweep: if the detector stops finding it, the sweep's zero is worthless and the tool refuses to publish.
Same decoy, asserted from the test side so that a broken detector fails the suite and not only the command.

A synthetic token of the right shape, never issued by anyone. Second positive control: the AWS form alone would not prove the Hugging Face form still fires, and that is the provider this repository actually depends on.
The PEM header line only, with no key material after it. It proves the detector still recognises a private key block by its header, which is how a real one would announce itself.

Historic only. An earlier version of THIS file quoted the AWS example key in the prose explaining why it is a decoy. The value is gone from HEAD, but a public repository forgets nothing — removing a string from the last commit does not remove it from the history. Declared rather than pretended away.

A synthetic Ed25519 key body, never generated by any keypair. It is the positive control for the form our own signing key would travel in — bare base64, no PEM header, as it would sit in an environment variable. Without it, the detector could stop recognising that form and nobody would know.
Same, for X25519. Its DER prefix differs from Ed25519 by two characters; one witness would not prove the other still fires.

Same, for RSA. This one matters more than the others: the RSA prefix is NOT constant — the modulus length byte moves — so its pattern anchors on the algorithm identifier instead, and this witness is what proves that anchoring still works.

A synthetic Stripe key. It exists because the OpenAI pattern requires `sk-` with a hyphen and Stripe writes `sk_live_` with an underscore: one character of difference made the pattern quietly false about a whole provider.
A synthetic Slack token of the `xoxe-` form, which the previous character class omitted.
A synthetic connection string with a password in it. Nothing about it looks like a key — no prefix, no fixed length — which is why it needs its own witness.

The PEM header line only, with no key material after it, in the case that proves the detector still knows the CURRENT formats of each provider. Invisible to the sweep until 2026-08-25, when `-m` was added: without it `git log -p` shows no diff for a merge commit, so anything introduced in a conflict resolution was never read.
A synthetic postgres URL with a made-up password, issued by nobody. Same case, same reason for its late appearance.
A synthetic Slack token of the right shape. Two forms match the same string — the plain one and the extended one — which is why it is declared twice.
Same string as above, matched by the wider pattern. Declaring only one of the two would leave the other undeclared and fail the check.

whyNoValuesHere: This file names forms, files and fingerprints. It never carries the value. A declarations file that quotes the strings it excuses is a file that ships secrets — and the sweep found this one doing exactly that, one pass after it was written.
